title: Maharashtra Minister's Niece Nila Vikhe Patil Elected to Swedish Parliament
excerpt: Green Party leader Nila Vikhe Patil, 41 - a former adviser in Sweden's Prime Minister's Office - won a Stockholm City seat in the Riksdag as the left opposition secured a narrow majority in the September 13 election.
body:
• Nila Vikhe Patil, 41, of Sweden's Green Party was elected to the 349-member Riksdag from the Stockholm City constituency in the September 13 general election; she takes office September 28.
  • Born in Lidköping, Sweden, and partly raised in Ahmednagar, Maharashtra, she is the niece of Maharashtra minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil and a former political adviser in Sweden's Prime Minister's Office.
  • The left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority in the election; Vikhe Patil brings 25 years of Green Party experience plus a consulting career at PwC to parliament.

Sweden's new parliament will include a familiar Indian surname. Nila Vikhe Patil, 41, of the Green Party (Miljöpartiet) has been elected to the Riksdag from the Stockholm City constituency in Sweden's September 13 general election — a Sweden-born politician from one of Maharashtra's most prominent political families who has spent a quarter-century in Swedish public life.

Vikhe Patil is the niece of Maharashtra minister Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil, the daughter of educationist Ashok Vikhe Patil, and the granddaughter of the late Union minister Balasaheb Vikhe Patil. Her great-grandfather, Vithalrao Vikhe Patil, founded Asia's first cooperative sugar factory. She was born in 1985 in Lidköping, Sweden, and spent her early childhood in Ahmednagar, Maharashtra — a dual upbringing that has shaped how she talks about her identity.

A political career, not just a family name

Indian coverage has understandably leaned on the family connection, but Vikhe Patil is no political newcomer. She has been in the Green Party for roughly 25 years, served as a political adviser in the Prime Minister's Office under Stefan Lofven — working on housing, tax and finance policy — and sat on the Stockholm City Council and the Stockholm Green Party's election committee.

Outside politics she has built a parallel professional career: she holds a bachelor's and an MBA from the Gothenburg School of Business, Economics and Law, studied at the Complutense University of Madrid, and has worked at PricewaterhouseCoopers since 2020 in management, technology and strategy consulting, becoming an authorized public accountant in 2025.

"It feels nice to be a part of the 349-member Parliament. I am looking forward to contributing to the city and the country."

— Nila Vikhe Patil, in an interview with PTI after her election

The election and what's ahead

Sweden votes every four years, and the 2026 election — following the 2022 contest — gave the left-leaning opposition a narrow majority. Vikhe Patil will assume office on September 28, representing Stockholm City in a parliament where coalition arithmetic will be tight and every seat counts.

Her stated priorities are children's welfare and the environment. "I would like to be a voice for those who cannot vote," she told PTI. "We need a habitable planet with clean water, living nature and as few human-caused natural disasters as possible." On her Indian roots, she said she hopes to make her grandfather proud: "He made me read the state budget when I was 15... I love India dearly and I feel very connected."

A diaspora milestone — with nuance

Indian-origin politicians remain rare in national parliaments across Scandinavia, so the election registers as a genuine diaspora milestone. But the framing cuts both ways. In India, the headline is the Maharashtra minister's niece entering a foreign parliament. In Sweden, Vikhe Patil is a Stockholm Green Party politician defined by her record on housing, tax and children's policy — and by a Swedish political career that predates this election by decades.

That asymmetry is worth holding onto. Diaspora success stories are often narrated through family names and origin myths; the substance underneath — 25 years of party work, an advisory role at the centre of government, a professional career in consulting — is what will determine whether the new Riksdag member from Stockholm City shapes policy or merely decorates it.
nri_angle: A Sweden-born politician of Maharashtra roots entering the Riksdag is a notable diaspora milestone, and a reminder of how Indian-origin careers in foreign public life are read differently at home and abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
